questions.explanation: The unknown pilot makes gestures from the cockpit suggesting that the narrator should follow.

questions.question: Why does the narrator follow the black aeroplane?
options: He hopes it will guide him safely out of the storm
He wants to race it
He recognises his friend flying it
He intends to attack it
questions.explanation: The mysterious pilot appears to offer a way through the dangerous clouds.

questions.question: How does the narrator feel when he realises his instruments have failed?
options: Frightened and helpless
Proud and relaxed
Bored
Certain of his exact location
questions.explanation: Losing his instruments and radio in the storm leaves him afraid and uncertain.

questions.question: What happens after the narrator follows the black aeroplane for some time?
options: He comes out of the clouds and sees the runway
He lands on a mountain
He returns to France without landing
He finds the aircraft has landed beside him
questions.explanation: The unknown plane guides him out of the storm toward the airport runway.

questions.question: What happens to the black aeroplane when the narrator reaches safety?
options: It disappears
It lands beside the Dakota
It turns into a helicopter
It follows him into the control tower
questions.explanation: When the narrator emerges from the clouds, the mysterious aircraft is no longer visible.

questions.question: What does the control tower tell the narrator about other aircraft in the sky?
options: No other aircraft was shown or reported in the sky
A large formation had escorted him
The black plane had landed first
The runway was closed to all traffic
questions.explanation: The control tower’s response makes the other plane’s presence mysterious.

questions.question: Why is the ending of ‘Black Aeroplane’ mysterious?
options: The narrator is guided by a plane that ground control says was not there
The narrator forgets the name of his aircraft
The control tower refuses to speak to him
The storm never ends
questions.explanation: The black plane helps him, yet the control tower reports no other plane in the sky.

questions.question: Which problem is the narrator’s most immediate challenge in the storm?
options: Navigating without working instruments or radio
Finding a meal
Communicating with passengers on a ship
Repairing the runway
questions.explanation: The failure of the compass, instruments and radio leaves him unable to navigate normally.

questions.question: What role does the black aeroplane play in the plot?
options: It appears to guide the narrator to safety
It causes the storm
It steals the Dakota
It takes the narrator back to France
questions.explanation: The mysterious aircraft leads the narrator through the clouds toward a safe landing.

questions.question: What does the pilot’s decision to enter the storm reveal?
options: He prioritises reaching home, despite a serious risk
He has no destination
He is ordered to ignore weather
He believes his instruments cannot fail
questions.explanation: His eagerness to reach home leads him to take a risky route into the clouds.

questions.question: Which literary element is most prominent at the end of ‘Black Aeroplane’?
options: Suspense and mystery
Comic misunderstanding about a letter
A resolved family argument
A detailed history of aviation
questions.explanation: The unexplained disappearance and the tower’s response leave the reader with a mystery.

questions.question: What does the narrator discover when the plane emerges from the storm?
options: The runway is ahead of him
His compass is permanently repaired
His family is waiting on the wing
The black aeroplane has landed nearby
questions.explanation: He sees the runway and is able to land safely.

questions.question: What is the significance of the narrator’s radio failure?
options: It cuts him off from advice and assistance from ground control
It makes the aircraft faster
It reveals the weather outside
It tells him the identity of the unknown pilot
questions.explanation: Without radio contact he cannot ask ground control for guidance.

questions.question: Which detail makes the black aeroplane seem unusual?
options: It appears in the storm and then vanishes without explanation
It has bright red wings described in detail
It lands at a busy airport
The narrator knows its pilot personally
questions.explanation: The aircraft’s unexplained appearance and disappearance create the mystery.

questions.question: What is the narrator’s attitude toward home before he enters the storm?
options: He is eager to be home with his family
He wants to avoid his family
He plans to stay in France forever
He is indifferent to his destination
questions.explanation: He is looking forward to his holiday and being with his family.

questions.question: Which statement best explains the narrator’s vulnerability in the storm?
options: His normal navigation and communication tools fail at the same time
He has no aircraft
He does not know what an aeroplane is
The airport refuses to accept him before take-off
questions.explanation: The loss of instruments and radio leaves him unable to navigate or ask for help.

questions.question: Which possible interpretation of the black aeroplane is supported by the story’s ambiguity?
options: It may be a mysterious or unexplained guide
It is definitely identified as a known military plane
It is confirmed to be the narrator’s own reflection
It is described as a dream by the control tower
questions.explanation: The story never explains the aircraft’s identity, leaving its appearance unresolved.

questions.question: Which mood is strongest while the narrator is inside the storm?
options: Tension and fear
Celebration
Boredom
Peaceful nostalgia
questions.explanation: The failed instruments and surrounding dark clouds create fear and suspense.

questions.question: What is the main theme of ‘Black Aeroplane’?
options: Facing danger and encountering an unexplained source of help
The value of farming
The harm caused by distrust of post office workers
The importance of family arguments
questions.explanation: The story centres on a pilot’s danger, his search for a way out and the mystery of his helper.

questions.question: What quality does the pilot display by continuing to act in the emergency?
options: Determination to find a safe route
A refusal to think
Carelessness toward every risk
A desire to abandon the aircraft
questions.explanation: He keeps flying and follows the apparent guide in an effort to reach safety.

questions.question: What do both stories have in common?
options: Characters face uncertainty and must act under pressure
Both are about a lost letter
Both take place inside a post office
Both describe a successful harvest
questions.explanation: The seagull and the pilot each face a frightening situation and must respond to it.

questions.question: How do the main characters’ challenges differ?
options: The seagull fears his first flight, while the pilot faces danger in a storm
The seagull loses a radio while the pilot loses his wings
Both characters are afraid of the sea for the same reason
The pilot is learning to fly for the first time
questions.explanation: One story focuses on a young bird’s fear; the other on a pilot’s navigation crisis.

questions.question: What helps the young seagull act, while the pilot follows the black plane?
options: The seagull is lured by food; the pilot hopes for guidance
Both receive written instructions
Both are carried by their parents
The seagull uses a radio and the pilot uses a fish
questions.explanation: Food motivates the bird’s leap, while the pilot sees the black plane as a possible guide.

questions.question: Which story ends with a clearer explanation of the central event?
options: His First Flight
Black Aeroplane
Both are equally unexplained
Neither has a central event
questions.explanation: The seagull’s fear is overcome through his first flight, while the identity of the black plane remains unexplained.

questions.question: Which story relies more heavily on an unresolved mystery?
options: Black Aeroplane
His First Flight
Both rely only on comedy
Neither uses mystery
questions.explanation: The mysterious aircraft disappears and is denied by the control tower, leaving the ending unexplained.

questions.question: What is the role of family support in ‘His First Flight’?
options: It helps the seagull face a challenge, even though he must take the leap himself
It makes the seagull permanently dependent
It prevents him from learning
It has no role in the plot
questions.explanation: His family encourages him, but he must make the attempt himself.

questions.question: Which choice best captures the shared lesson of the two stories?
options: Facing a difficult situation may require courage and a willingness to act
Every problem can be solved by ignoring it
Fear proves that success is impossible
Only technology can help people
questions.explanation: Both stories show characters responding to fear or danger rather than simply giving up.

questions.question: Which is a key difference between the stories’ settings?
options: One takes place around a cliff and sea; the other in an aircraft flying through storm clouds
Both take place in a school
One is set in a post office and one in a courtroom
Both occur in a city market
questions.explanation: The seagull story is set around its coastal home; the pilot story unfolds in the sky during a storm.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the young seagull’s first leap?
options: It begins as a response to hunger but becomes a discovery of his ability
It is a carefully planned flight lesson
It is caused by the black aeroplane
It is unrelated to the mother’s actions
questions.explanation: The fish draws him into a leap, after which he discovers that his wings can support him.

questions.question: Which detail explains the pilot’s growing uncertainty?
options: He cannot use his compass or radio inside the clouds
He can see the runway from the start
The aircraft has no fuel before he reaches the storm
He is accompanied by his family
questions.explanation: The equipment failures leave him unable to determine his direction or contact ground control.

questions.question: What makes the pilot’s safe landing surprising?
options: The mysterious guide disappears and the tower reports no other plane
He lands at the wrong airport
His aircraft is carried by a bird
The storm turns into a clear morning before take-off
questions.explanation: The successful guidance conflicts with the control tower’s information that there was no other aircraft.

questions.question: What is the best interpretation of the seagull’s change from fear to excitement?
options: Experience gives him confidence that reassurance alone had not provided
He discovers that flight is impossible
His siblings make him afraid of food
He decides he no longer needs his wings
questions.explanation: Once he flies, he learns his own ability and feels triumphant.

questions.question: Which narrative technique is especially important in ‘Black Aeroplane’?
options: First-person narration that places readers inside the pilot’s uncertainty
A series of letters written by the control tower
A narrator who knows the unknown pilot’s identity
A chorus of seagulls telling the story
questions.explanation: The narrator recounts his own frightening flight, allowing readers to share his uncertainty.

questions.question: Which statement best summarises ‘His First Flight’?
options: A frightened young seagull is tempted by food, takes his first flight and gains confidence
A pilot loses his way in a storm and follows a black plane
A farmer writes to God after losing his crop
A family travels by train to the sea
questions.explanation: The story follows the young bird from fear of flying to a successful first flight.

questions.question: Which statement best summarises ‘Black Aeroplane’?
options: A pilot lost in a storm follows an unknown aircraft to safety, then learns the tower saw no other plane
A young bird learns to fly with help from its mother
A farmer receives money from a postmaster
A pilot chooses to cancel a flight before take-off
questions.explanation: The story centres on the mysterious aircraft that appears to guide the narrator through the storm.

questions.question: What is a reasonable lesson from the seagull’s experience?
options: People may discover strengths by attempting what frightens them
Waiting forever is the safest way to learn
Support means doing every task for someone else
A first attempt must be perfect
questions.explanation: The young bird learns by taking action despite fear.

questions.question: What is a reasonable lesson from the pilot’s experience?
options: In a crisis, assess risks and seek a path to safety
Ignore all warning signs
Turn off every instrument before flying
Assume every unexplained event is harmless
questions.explanation: The story shows the danger of entering a storm and the pilot’s need to find a safe route out.

questions.question: Which detail is most important for understanding the seagull’s motivation?
options: The fish is just beyond his reach
The control tower reports no aircraft
The pilot’s fuel gauge is faulty
The old Dakota is returning to England
questions.explanation: The fish provides the immediate incentive that makes him leap toward it.

questions.question: Which detail is most important for understanding the black plane’s mystery?
options: The tower reports that no other aircraft is in the sky
The narrator is flying home
The plane is an old Dakota
The clouds are dark
questions.explanation: The tower’s statement contradicts the narrator’s experience of being guided by another plane.

questions.question: Which phrase best describes the emotional arc of ‘His First Flight’?
options: Fear changes into confidence and joy
Pride changes into permanent despair
Anger changes into revenge
Boredom changes into indifference
questions.explanation: The young seagull moves from fear to a triumphant discovery of flight.

questions.question: Which phrase best describes the emotional arc of ‘Black Aeroplane’?
options: Anticipation turns into fear, then relief and mystery
Joy turns into anger over a letter
Boredom turns into a harvest celebration
Confidence turns into a public speech
questions.explanation: The pilot begins excited about going home, becomes frightened in the storm, then lands safely with an unexplained question remaining.

questions.question: Why is the ending of ‘Black Aeroplane’ not a fully resolved ending?
options: The identity and existence of the guiding aircraft remain unexplained
The narrator never reaches a runway
The tower refuses to answer any question
The pilot loses his family
questions.explanation: The plane’s unexplained appearance and disappearance leave the mystery open.

questions.question: Which conclusion about the two protagonists is best supported?
options: Both move from a difficult moment toward safety or success by responding to the situation
Both refuse to act
Both rely on letters rather than action
Both have the same fear of flying
questions.explanation: The seagull succeeds in flight and the pilot reaches the runway after following the mysterious plane.

questions.question: Which skill does the young seagull gain through his experience?
options: Independent flight
Using a compass
Communicating by radio
Navigating a runway
questions.explanation: He learns to fly rather than remain dependent on the ledge.

questions.question: Which tool fails the pilot inside the storm, making navigation difficult?
options: The compass
A fishing net
A telescope used on land
A ship’s anchor
questions.explanation: The compass and other flight instruments fail within the clouds.

questions.question: Which detail most clearly establishes that the narrator is an experienced pilot rather than a novice learning to fly?
options: He is piloting his old Dakota on a return journey to England
He is a young seagull on a ledge
He needs his mother to bring fish
He has never seen an aeroplane
questions.explanation: The narrator is already flying an aircraft on a journey home, unlike the young seagull learning to fly.

questions.question: Which theme is shared by both stories even though the settings differ?
options: Dealing with fear and uncertainty
The unfairness of a post office
The history of South African democracy
The importance of a good harvest
questions.explanation: Both narratives centre on characters facing frightening or uncertain situations.

questions.question: What does the mother’s use of food show about support?
options: Support can encourage someone to act while leaving the decisive action to them
Support always means removing every challenge
Support requires punishment only
Support is unrelated to motivation
questions.explanation: She makes the fish a motivation, but the young seagull must launch himself.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why the pilot trusts the black aeroplane enough to follow it?
options: He is lost and the other pilot appears to signal a way through the clouds
He knows the other pilot personally
The control tower orders him to follow
The other pilot sends a written route
questions.explanation: In a dangerous situation with failed instruments, he follows the apparent guide to find a way out.

questions.question: Which type of conflict is central to ‘His First Flight’?
options: The young bird’s internal struggle with fear
A political conflict between countries
A dispute about a land boundary
A mystery about a postmaster
questions.explanation: The main obstacle is his own fear of taking flight.

questions.question: Which type of conflict is central to ‘Black Aeroplane’?
options: A pilot struggles against dangerous weather and uncertainty
A young bird argues with its siblings about food
A family debates moving house
A farmer faces a crop disease
questions.explanation: The storm and failed instruments create an external crisis for the pilot.

questions.question: Which is the strongest reason the two stories are presented together?
options: They explore flight through different challenges: fear in one and danger in the other
They share the same protagonist
They both explain the construction of aircraft
They are both written as letters
questions.explanation: One focuses on a young bird’s first flight; the other on a pilot’s dangerous flight through a storm.

questions.question: What does ‘His First Flight’ imply about learning a new skill?
options: A difficult first attempt can become the start of confidence
Success occurs only without effort
Advice makes practice unnecessary
Fear always means a person lacks ability
questions.explanation: The seagull learns by acting and discovering his wings can support him.

title: From the Diary of Anne Frank

questions.question: Why does Anne decide to write a diary?
options: She wants to publish a newspaper
She needs a trusted listener for thoughts she cannot easily share
Her teacher orders a daily report
She wants to record only school marks
questions.explanation: Anne treats the diary as a confidante who will listen without judging.

questions.question: Anne’s classroom episode involving Mr Keesing mainly shows her:
options: Inability to write
Humour and creativity when responding to criticism
Dislike of all subjects
Decision to leave school
questions.explanation: Her playful essays turn the teacher’s complaint into a comic exchange.

questions.question: A diary can be valuable because it:
options: Automatically makes every opinion correct
Records personal experiences and changing reflections
Replaces all historical evidence
Must be written for an audience
questions.explanation: A diary preserves a personal viewpoint over time.

questions.question: On what occasion did Anne receive her diary?
options: Her thirteenth birthday
Her first day at university
Her family’s return to Germany
A school prize ceremony
questions.explanation: Anne receives the diary as a birthday present shortly before beginning the entries shown in the chapter.

questions.question: Why does Anne feel she can confide in a diary more easily than in people?
options: She wants a listener who will not judge or interrupt her
She has been ordered to stop speaking to everyone
She dislikes writing
She expects the diary to give her school marks
questions.explanation: She wants a friend-like listener with whom she can share her thoughts honestly.

questions.question: What name does Anne give to her diary?
options: Kitty
Margot
Sanne
Mrs Kuperus
questions.explanation: Anne addresses her diary as Kitty, treating it like a personal friend.

questions.question: What does Anne say is missing from her life despite having family and acquaintances?
options: A true friend with whom she can share her inner thoughts
A place to live
A school to attend
A collection of books
questions.explanation: Anne feels she lacks a close friend to whom she can confide freely.

questions.question: What kind of writing does Anne want her diary to be?
options: A friend-like confidante rather than a list of facts
A science textbook
A public timetable
A set of school examination answers
questions.explanation: She wants the diary to function as a friend, not simply record factual events.

questions.question: Why does Anne briefly introduce her family and background in her diary?
options: To help Kitty understand the people she mentions
To submit a school assignment
To explain how to write a newspaper
To provide instructions for her teacher
questions.explanation: She gives background so that the diary’s imagined reader can follow her personal account.

questions.question: What does Anne’s decision to address the diary as Kitty show?
options: She personifies the diary as a trusted companion
She believes the diary is a real teacher
She wants her diary to be anonymous in class
She is writing a letter to her sister
questions.explanation: The name Kitty helps Anne imagine the diary as a friend who will listen to her.

questions.question: Which quality is especially evident in Anne’s writing?
options: Self-awareness and a lively sense of humour
Complete indifference to others
A refusal to reflect on her behaviour
An inability to express opinions
questions.explanation: Anne reflects on her feelings and uses humour to describe her experiences.

questions.question: How does Anne generally view her own talkativeness?
options: She recognises it as a habit and tries to explain it
She denies ever talking in class
She blames it entirely on her sister
She thinks it makes her unable to write
questions.explanation: Anne admits that she talks a great deal and tries to defend or understand the habit.

questions.question: Which teacher is annoyed by Anne’s talking in class?
options: Mr Keesing
Mr Barua
Mr Dussel
Mr Van Daan
questions.explanation: Mr Keesing, her mathematics teacher, objects to Anne’s talking during lessons.

questions.question: What subject does Mr Keesing teach?
options: Mathematics
History
Art
Music
questions.explanation: Anne identifies Mr Keesing as her mathematics teacher.

questions.question: What does Mr Keesing ask Anne to write as a punishment at first?
options: An essay about being a chatterbox
A poem about flying
A letter to the headteacher
A diary about her family
questions.explanation: He assigns an essay on the topic ‘A Chatterbox’ as a response to her talking.

questions.question: What is the title of Anne’s second assigned essay?
options: An Incorrigible Chatterbox
A Letter to God
The Black Aeroplane
The Quiet Student
questions.explanation: After the first essay, Mr Keesing assigns ‘An Incorrigible Chatterbox’.

questions.question: What does the word ‘incorrigible’ mean in the essay title?
options: Difficult or impossible to correct
Very quiet and shy
Highly skilled at mathematics
Always punctual
questions.explanation: The word describes a habit considered impossible to correct.

questions.question: What is the title of the third essay Mr Keesing assigns?
options: Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox
The Day I Stopped Talking
A Bird’s First Flight
A Visit to Amsterdam
questions.explanation: The third punishment essay receives the deliberately comic title about a chatterbox.

questions.question: Why does Mr Keesing keep assigning essays to Anne?
options: She continues talking during his lessons
She refuses to do any homework
She has damaged his books
She arrives late every day
questions.explanation: He uses writing assignments as a punishment for her continued talking in class.

questions.question: How does Anne justify her talkativeness in her first essay?
options: She suggests it is a trait that may be inherited from her mother
She says the teacher cannot hear her
She claims the classroom is too small
She says she does not understand language
questions.explanation: Anne argues that her mother is also talkative, so the habit may be inherited.

questions.question: What does Anne’s response to Mr Keesing show about her?
options: She can use humour and reasoning to defend herself
She accepts every criticism without thought

options: A sudden miracle without work
A process built through curiosity, practice and questioning
A result of luck alone
Something possible only for adults
questions.explanation: The account highlights habits and persistence rather than a single moment of genius.

questions.question: Mathilde’s dissatisfaction is driven largely by:
options: A wish to help the poor
Her longing for status and luxury beyond her means
A love of gardening
A fear of travelling
questions.explanation: She imagines a more luxurious social life than her circumstances allow.

questions.question: The necklace’s loss leads to:
options: A short holiday
Years of hardship to replace the jewellery
Immediate wealth
A new career in theatre
questions.explanation: The couple borrow heavily and work for years to repay the debt.

questions.question: The final revelation is ironic because:
options: The necklace was never worn
The original necklace was imitation jewellery, worth far less than the replacement
Mathilde becomes a queen
The party never occurred
questions.explanation: The sacrifice was based on a mistaken assumption about the necklace’s value.

questions.question: Education changes Bholi chiefly by helping her:
options: Become wealthy overnight
Gain confidence and speak up for her dignity
Forget her family
Avoid all responsibility
questions.explanation: Schooling gives Bholi confidence to resist an unequal marriage arrangement.

questions.question: Bholi refuses the proposed marriage when the groom:
options: Offers a kind gift
Demands money after seeing her
Asks her to study
Arrives late
questions.explanation: His demand for dowry exposes his greed and leads her to reject the match.

questions.question: The teacher is important because she:
options: Mocks Bholi’s speech
Offers encouragement and a safe path to learning
Arranges the dowry
Forbids her to speak
questions.explanation: The teacher’s patience helps Bholi begin to believe in herself.

title: The Book That Saved the Earth

questions.question: Think-Tank misinterprets the book because he:
options: Reads every word carefully
Assumes nursery rhymes are evidence of Earth’s military power
Cannot see the book
Has already visited Earth
questions.explanation: His ignorance and arrogance turn harmless rhymes into supposed threats.

questions.question: The play creates comedy through:
options: Accurate scientific reporting
Miscommunication and overconfident conclusions
A realistic battlefield
A serious courtroom
questions.explanation: The Martians’ misunderstanding of ordinary text drives the comic plot.

questions.question: The play’s central lesson is that:
options: Loud confidence guarantees wisdom
Lack of context can lead to absurd conclusions
Books are always dangerous
Technology removes all misunderstanding
questions.explanation: Think-Tank’s rash interpretations show the danger of jumping to conclusions.

questions.question: A passage says a town planted trees and summer temperatures later fell. Which conclusion is safest?
options: Trees certainly caused every temperature change
Tree planting may have contributed; other evidence would strengthen the claim
The temperature record is irrelevant
Trees always lower every climate measurement
questions.explanation: A careful inference recognises a plausible link without claiming proof beyond the evidence.

questions.question: Which detail best supports the claim that a narrator is unreliable?
options: The narrator openly admits uncertainty
The narrator’s account contradicts independently established facts
The narrator uses short sentences
The story has a title
questions.explanation: Contradictions between the account and reliable evidence can indicate unreliability.

questions.question: The main idea of a passage is best identified by:
options: Choosing the first sentence automatically
Combining the central point with the supporting details
Selecting the longest word
Using only the final example
questions.explanation: The main idea summarises the passage’s central point rather than one detail.

questions.question: A word’s meaning in context is best inferred from:
options: Its spelling alone
The surrounding sentence and passage
The number of letters
Its position on a page
questions.explanation: Context clues help determine which meaning fits the use.

questions.question: Choose the correct determiner: There isn’t ___ milk left in the carton.
options: many
much
few
several
questions.explanation: ‘Milk’ is uncountable, so ‘much’ fits a negative sentence.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: Each student must bring ___ own notebook.
options: their
these
those
many
questions.explanation: Singular ‘their’ is an accepted gender-neutral determiner in contemporary English.

questions.question: There are ___ apples in the basket, enough for everyone.
options: little
much
several
any
questions.explanation: ‘Apples’ is countable plural, and ‘several’ indicates more than a few.

questions.question: I have read ___ of the two books, but not both.
options: neither
either
every
much
questions.explanation: ‘Either’ refers to one or the other of two choices.

questions.question: By the time we arrived, the film ___.
options: starts
has started
had started
will start
questions.explanation: The past perfect marks an event completed before another past event.

questions.question: She ___ at this school since 2022.
options: works
worked
has been working
will work
questions.explanation: The present perfect continuous describes an activity continuing from the past until now.

questions.question: If water reaches 100°C at standard pressure, it ___.
options: boiled
boils
will have boiled
is boiling yesterday
questions.explanation: The simple present expresses a general scientific fact.

questions.question: At 8 p.m. tomorrow, we ___ for the exam.
options: revised
will be revising
have revised
revise
questions.explanation: The future continuous describes an action in progress at a future time.

questions.question: You ___ wear a helmet while riding a motorcycle; it is a safety requirement.
options: might
must
would
could
questions.explanation: ‘Must’ expresses a strong obligation.

questions.question: ___ I borrow your dictionary for a moment?
options: May
Must
Should
Need
questions.explanation: ‘May I…?’ politely asks for permission.

questions.question: You look tired. You ___ take a short break.
options: should
mustn’t
cannot
needn’t have
questions.explanation: ‘Should’ gives advice rather than an absolute command.

questions.question: It ___ rain later; the forecast is uncertain.
options: must
might
need
ought
questions.explanation: ‘Might’ expresses possibility without certainty.

questions.question: Neither of the answers ___ correct.
options: are
were
is
have
questions.explanation: ‘Neither’ is treated as singular in this construction.

questions.question: The bouquet of roses ___ on the table.
options: are
is
were
have
questions.explanation: The subject is ‘bouquet’, not the plural noun ‘roses’.

questions.question: Each of the players ___ a numbered jersey.
options: have
has
are having
were
questions.explanation: ‘Each’ takes a singular verb.

questions.question: The news ___ surprising.
options: are
were
is
have
questions.explanation: ‘News’ is grammatically singular despite ending in -s.

questions.question: Direct: He said, “I am tired.” Choose the correct report.
options: He said that I am tired.
He said that he was tired.
He says that he had tired.
He told that he is tired.
questions.explanation: With a past reporting verb, ‘am’ usually backshifts to ‘was’ and the pronoun changes.

questions.question: Direct: The teacher said to me, “Please close the door.”
options: The teacher said me close the door.
The teacher requested me to close the door.
The teacher told that please close the door.
The teacher asked that I closed the door.
questions.explanation: A polite request is commonly reported with ‘requested + object + to-infinitive’.

questions.question: Direct: She asked, “Where do you live?”
options: She asked where did I live.
She asked where I lived.
She asked where do I live.
She asked that where I live.
questions.explanation: Reported questions use statement word order and usually backshift the tense.

questions.question: Direct: Ravi said, “I will call you tomorrow.”
options: Ravi said that he would call me the next day.
Ravi said he will call you tomorrow.
Ravi told that I call him yesterday.
Ravi asked if he called me.
questions.explanation: ‘Will’ commonly changes to ‘would’, ‘I’ to ‘he’, and ‘tomorrow’ to ‘the next day’.

questions.question: Choose the correction: “She do not like cold tea.”
options: do → does
like → likes
cold → colder
tea → teas
questions.explanation: With singular third-person subject ‘she’, use ‘does not’.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: “The results ___ announced yesterday.”
options: is
was
were
has
questions.explanation: ‘Results’ is plural and the sentence is in the past passive.

questions.question: Choose the best connector: “It was raining heavily, ___ the match continued.”
options: because
yet
unless
so that
questions.explanation: ‘Yet’ shows contrast between the heavy rain and the continuation of the match.

questions.question: Choose the correct preposition: “She is interested ___ astronomy.”
options: on
at
in
for
questions.explanation: The standard expression is ‘interested in’.

questions.question: A formal complaint letter should generally use:
options: Personal insults
Clear facts, a polite tone and a specific request
Only slang
No date or subject
questions.explanation: Effective formal letters are courteous, precise and action-oriented.

questions.question: The subject line of a formal email should be:
options: A full paragraph
Brief and informative
A greeting only
Left blank in every case
questions.explanation: A concise subject helps the recipient understand the purpose immediately.

questions.question: Which closing is suitable for a formal letter when the recipient’s name is unknown?
options: Lots of love
Yours faithfully
See ya
Cheers mate
questions.explanation: ‘Yours faithfully’ is a conventional formal closing when the recipient is not named.

questions.question: When writing to a civic authority about a damaged road, the strongest evidence is:
options: An unrelated personal opinion
Location, dates, specific safety concerns and a clear request
An exaggerated accusation
A poem about roads
questions.explanation: Specific verifiable details make the request clearer and more actionable.

questions.question: When describing a chart, a strong opening sentence should:
options: List every number randomly
State the overall trend or main comparison
Add facts not shown
Give a personal anecdote instead
questions.explanation: An analytical paragraph begins with the main pattern before details.

questions.question: If a value rises from 40 to 50, the percentage increase is:
questions.explanation: The increase is 10; 10/40 × 100 = 25%.

questions.question: Which phrase is most appropriate for comparing data?
options: The chart proves without doubt
By contrast, the figure for…
Everyone knows that
I personally feel the bar is
questions.explanation: ‘By contrast’ clearly signals a comparison between values.

questions.question: A good analytical paragraph should:
options: Repeat every label
Select relevant comparisons and support them with data
Invent possible causes as facts
Avoid an overall conclusion
questions.explanation: It summarises key patterns, uses evidence and avoids unsupported claims.
